focus: Public effectiveness rests on private credibility and trust balances; relationships need deposits before difficult cooperation can survive withdrawals, mistakes, or conflict.
coreClaim: Interdependence becomes possible only when independent people build trust through understanding, small courtesies, kept commitments, clarified expectations, integrity, and sincere repair.

centralConcept.name: Emotional Bank Account
centralConcept.plainDefinition: The Emotional Bank Account is a trust balance in a relationship. Deposits are actions that build confidence and goodwill; withdrawals are actions that create suspicion, resentment, or caution.
centralConcept.whyItMatters: A reader who uses the metaphor sees relationship problems as capacity problems, not just communication events. High trust makes later disagreement workable; low trust makes even neutral words feel threatening.

keyClaims: Private Victory precedes Public Victory because self-discipline and self-mastery create the reliability other people can trust.
Independence is a prerequisite for interdependence, but independence alone cannot produce the highest family, team, or organizational results.
Trust functions like an account balance: repeated deposits create room for mistakes, while repeated withdrawals make every interaction expensive.
Understanding the individual comes before all other deposits because a gesture counts as a deposit only if it matters to the other person.
Little kindnesses and courtesies are large in relationships because small disrespect often communicates deeper disregard.
Kept commitments, clarified expectations, personal integrity, and sincere apology each prevent or repair predictable withdrawals.
Every production problem in an interdependent setting can become a production-capability opportunity when handled in a way that builds trust.

namedExamples.label: Emotional Bank Account
namedExamples.summary: Trust is compared to an account that can hold a high or low balance. When the balance is high, communication is easy and mistakes are forgiven; when the balance is low, every word is interpreted defensively.
namedExamples.teachesWhat: Relationship capacity must be built before difficult collaboration is demanded.

namedExamples.label: Six major deposits
namedExamples.summary: The trust-building deposits are understanding the individual, attending to little things, keeping commitments, clarifying expectations, showing personal integrity, and apologizing sincerely after a withdrawal. Each deposit targets a common source of relational breakdown.
namedExamples.teachesWhat: Trust grows through specific repeated behaviors rather than vague goodwill.

namedExamples.label: Six-year-old interruption during important work
namedExamples.summary: A child interrupts an adult engaged in a high-priority project with something that appears trivial from the adult viewpoint. If the concern matters deeply to the child, giving attention can become a major deposit because the relationship matters more than the task rhythm.
namedExamples.teachesWhat: Understanding the other person's priority determines whether an action is a deposit or a withdrawal.

namedExamples.label: Dag Hammarskjöld and one-person service
namedExamples.summary: The former United Nations Secretary-General is invoked to elevate full attention to one person over abstract service to masses. The example keeps public victory grounded in concrete one-to-one relationships.
namedExamples.teachesWhat: Grand ideals do not excuse neglecting the person directly in front of you.

hardEdge: The surface takeaway is to be courteous so people will cooperate later. The harder point is capacity before production: trust is not decoration around teamwork but the condition that makes disagreement, correction, and shared results possible.
voiceCues: uses a financial metaphor to make invisible trust balances measurable
lists deposits in practical relationship language rather than abstract virtue alone
bridges private discipline to public cooperation with a threshold claim
treats problems as opportunities to build capacity when handled with principle
paraphraseNotes: The public section starts by slowing the move toward other people. Self-mastery comes first because relationships expose private inconsistency. A person who cannot keep promises internally will struggle to create dependable trust externally. The Emotional Bank Account supplies the operating metaphor. Every interaction deposits or withdraws from a relationship's trust balance, and the balance changes how messages are received. With a high balance, mistakes are interpreted generously and communication remains flexible. With a low balance, even careful words are filtered through suspicion. Six deposits are named with practical specificity. Understanding the individual is first because a deposit must be meaningful to the receiver, not merely convenient to the giver. Attending to little things matters because small discourtesies often signal large disregard. Keeping commitments is a major deposit because broken promises create deep withdrawals. Clarifying expectations prevents the hidden contracts that later become resentment. Showing personal integrity includes loyalty to absent people, since present listeners learn whether their own reputation is safe. Sincere apology repairs withdrawals when it is specific and not repeated as a substitute for changed behavior. The section also reframes P problems as PC opportunities: a conflict, mistake, or disappointment can either deplete trust or build it, depending on how it is handled. The result is a bridge from independence to interdependence through earned relational capacity.
